plain: Computers doing tasks we used to think needed a person, like reading, seeing or deciding.
Getting a computer to learn a task from examples instead of being told every rule.
The thing that learns: a recipe of maths plus the numbers (weights) it has learned.
One number a model learns; a model is mostly a big pile of weights.
aka: Not an event weight: a weight here is a number the model learns

plain: An extra number added after the weights, so a layer can shift its answer up or down.
aka: Offset, intercept. Not a statistical bias: see Bias (statistics)

plain: Any number the model learns while training: its weights and biases.
A setting you choose before training, like the learning rate or the batch size; the model does not learn it.
A block of numbers with a shape, such as a picture of 28 x 28 numbers.
How many numbers a tensor has along each side, written like [64, 1, 28, 28].
One measured fact about an example, like a pixel's brightness or a person's age.
The right answer that comes with a training example, like 'this digit is a 7'.
The collection of examples a model learns from and is tested on.

full: Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology (digits)
plain: 70,000 small pictures of hand-written digits, the classic first dataset for learning ML.
Showing a model examples and nudging its weights so its answers get better.
Using a trained model to answer new questions; nothing is learned any more.
aka: Prediction (ML). In statistics and HEP, 'inference' means estimating parameters from data: see Statistical inference

plain: Learning from examples that come with the right answers.
Finding patterns in data that has no right answers attached, like grouping similar pictures.
Making the answers from the data itself, like hiding a word and predicting it.
Choosing which group something belongs to, like which digit a picture shows.
Predicting a number, like a price or an energy, rather than a group.
One number saying how wrong the model is; training tries to make it smaller.
aka: Cost, objective; chi-square or −log L in HEP fits

plain: The rule that turns the model's answers and the right answers into the loss.
For every weight, which way and how strongly to change it to lower the loss.
Working out every weight's gradient by going backwards through the model from the loss.
Training by stepping every weight a little against its gradient, over and over.
Gradient descent on small random batches of examples instead of all the data at once.
A popular optimizer that gives each weight its own step size from its recent gradients.
Adam with weight decay applied separately, the usual way to train transformers.
The rule that uses the gradients to change the weights, such as SGD or Adam.
How big a step the optimizer takes each time; too small crawls, too big bounces.
Changing the learning rate during training, such as warming up then slowly lowering it.
Starting training with a small learning rate and raising it, to avoid an unstable start.
Letting each step keep some of the previous step's direction, like a rolling ball.
A group of examples processed together in one training step.
How many examples go into one step; it changes how noisy each step is.
One full pass through all the training examples.
One update of the weights: one batch in, one change out.
The starting values of the weights before training; a bad start can stop learning.
Learning the training examples so closely that the model does worse on new ones.
A model too simple, or trained too little, to capture the pattern at all.
How well a model does on examples it has never seen.
Any trick that keeps a model from overfitting, such as weight decay or dropout.
aka: Penalty term; a prior, in Bayesian words

plain: Pulling every weight a little towards zero each step, to keep the model simple.
aka: L2 penalty; a Gaussian prior on the weights

plain: Penalties on the size of the weights: L1 pushes some to exactly zero, L2 shrinks them all.
Switching random neurons off during training, so the model cannot rely on any one.
Stopping training when the score on held-out data stops improving.
Making extra training examples by changing the real ones a little, like shifting a picture.
Three separate piles of data: one to learn from, one to tune settings, one for the final honest score.
Testing on each part of the data in turn while training on the rest, for a fairer score.
Examples kept away from training so they can test the model fairly.
The share of answers that are right.
Of the things the model said 'yes' to, the share that really were yes.
Of the things that really were yes, the share the model found.
aka: Signal efficiency, true positive rate, sensitivity

plain: One number that balances precision and recall (their harmonic mean).

full: True Positive / False Positive / True Negative / False Negative
plain: The four ways a yes-or-no answer can be right or wrong.
aka: In HEP: signal kept, background kept, background rejected, signal lost

plain: A table counting which answers the model gave for each true answer.
A curve of found-right against false alarms as you move the yes/no threshold.
aka: In HEP often drawn as background rejection against signal efficiency

plain: The area under the ROC curve: 1 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing.
The area under a precision-recall curve; mAP averages it over classes. Used to score detectors.
Whether a model's confidence matches how often it is right; 80% sure should be right 80% of the time.
aka: Not HEP calibration (correcting a detector): see Calibration (HEP)

plain: The cut-off that turns a score into a yes or no.
The trade-off between a model too simple to fit (bias) and one too jumpy to trust (variance).
Test error that falls, rises, then falls again as models get bigger.
One unit in a layer: it adds up its weighted inputs, adds a bias and applies an activation.
One stage of a network that turns its input numbers into new numbers.
A layer where every output is a weighted sum of every input, plus a bias.
A bend applied after a layer (like ReLU) so a network can learn more than straight lines.
The simplest activation: keep positive numbers, turn negative ones into 0.
A smooth cousin of ReLU, used in GPT-2 and most transformers.
An S-shaped squash that turns any number into one between 0 and 1.
Turns a list of scores into chances that add up to 1.
The raw scores a model gives before softmax turns them into chances.
The usual loss for choosing between classes: how surprised the model is by the right answer.
Cross-entropy for yes-or-no answers.
The average of the squared differences between answers and right answers.
The average size of the mistakes, ignoring their sign.
A network of linear layers with activations between them, the simplest deep network.
aka: DNN (common in HEP), fully connected network, feed-forward network

plain: Any neural network with several layers.
aka: In HEP usually means an MLP: a fully connected network

plain: Machine learning with neural networks of many layers.
A model made of layers of simple units, loosely inspired by brain cells.
Rescaling numbers inside a network so they stay a sensible size; it makes training steadier.
aka: Not HEP normalisation (a distribution's overall size): see Normalisation (HEP)

plain: Normalising each feature using the average over the batch.
Normalising each example's numbers across its own features; used in transformers.
A simpler layer norm that only rescales, without subtracting the mean.
Adding a layer's input back to its output, so information and gradients flow easily through deep networks.
A list of numbers that stands for a thing (a word, a picture, a face) so similar things get similar numbers.
The small set of numbers a model squeezes its input into.
A narrow layer that forces the model to keep only what matters.
A network for pictures that slides small filters over the image instead of connecting every pixel.
Sliding a small grid of weights over a picture and taking a weighted sum at each place.
The small grid of weights a convolution slides over the picture.
How many pixels the filter moves each time; stride 2 halves the picture.
Extra pixels added round the edge so a convolution can keep the picture's size.
Shrinking a picture by keeping the biggest (max) or the average value of each small square.
Spreading a filter's taps apart so it sees a wider area with the same weights.
One layer of a picture's numbers, like red, green or blue, or one learned feature map.
The picture a filter makes: where in the input its pattern appears.
The patch of the original picture that one output number can see.
A convolution run backwards to make a picture bigger (upsampling).
Making a picture bigger or smaller.
False patterns that appear when fine detail is shrunk without blurring first.
A convolution that filters each channel on its own, using far fewer weights.
A convolution that only mixes channels at each pixel.
A network shaped like a U: it shrinks a picture, then grows it back, with shortcuts across.
A transformer that reads a picture as a sequence of small patches.
Finding things in a picture and drawing a box round each one.
The rectangle round a found object, given by four numbers.
How much two boxes overlap: the shared area divided by the area they cover together.
Removing duplicate boxes on the same object, keeping only the surest.
Labelling every pixel of a picture with what it belongs to.
Deciding whether two face photos show the same person.
Deciding which of a set of known people a face belongs to, or none.

full: False Accept Rate / False Reject Rate
plain: How often a check wrongly lets a stranger in, and how often it wrongly turns away the right person.
The error rate where false accepts and false rejects are equally common.
A loss that pulls two examples of the same thing together and pushes a different one away.
Learning embeddings by bringing matching pairs together and pushing others apart.
A contrastive loss: pick the right partner out of a batch of wrong ones.
Wrong examples that look very like the right one; they make contrastive training harder and better.
How closely two lists of numbers point the same way, from -1 to 1.
A store of embeddings that can quickly find the ones nearest to a question.
Finding nearly the nearest vectors much faster by not checking every one.
A layered graph that finds near neighbours by hopping from point to point.
Grouping vectors into lists and only searching the few lists nearest the question.
Fetching relevant text and putting it in front of a language model before it answers.
Finding the few directions along which data varies most, to describe it with fewer numbers.
Grouping points into k clusters, each around its average.

full: t-distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding / Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
plain: Ways to draw high-dimensional data in 2D, keeping neighbours near each other.
A classic classifier that draws the widest possible gap between two classes.
A model that answers by asking a chain of yes/no questions about the features.
Many decision trees, each trained on a random sample, voting together.
Building trees one after another, each fixing the previous ones' mistakes.
A fast, popular library for boosted trees.
Boosted trees, as physicists often call them.
How unpredictable something is, measured in bits.
How mixed the classes in a group are; trees split to make groups purer.
How different one set of probabilities is from another.
Choosing the settings that make the observed data most likely.
aka: Maximum likelihood fit (HEP); minimising cross-entropy is one (ML)

plain: The rule for updating a belief when new evidence arrives.
A model of smooth curves that also says how unsure it is between the data points.
aka: Kriging; used in HEP for smooth background fits

plain: How often chance alone would give a result at least this extreme.
A number measuring how far data are from a fitted curve, allowing for the errors.
A network that squeezes its input into a small code and rebuilds it from that code.
aka: Used in HEP for model-independent anomaly searches

plain: The part of a model that turns an input into a compact code or embedding.
The part of a model that turns a code back into data, such as a picture or text.
An autoencoder whose codes are kept smooth and random-like, so new examples can be drawn from them.
The quantity a VAE maximises: rebuild well, while keeping the codes close to random noise.
Two networks in a contest: a generator makes fakes and a judge (discriminator) tries to spot them.
The part of a GAN that turns random numbers into made-up examples.
The judge in a GAN: it scores whether an example is real or made up.
When a GAN's generator makes only a few kinds of output instead of the full variety.
A model that learns to remove noise step by step, so it can turn pure noise into a picture.
Two ways of running a diffusion model's steps: many random ones, or fewer fixed ones.
Pushing a diffusion model harder towards what was asked for, at some cost to variety.
A model that reshapes simple noise into data through steps that can be run backwards exactly.
An autoencoder whose codes are picked from a fixed list of learned vectors.
Grouping data into clusters inside an autoencoder's code space.
Data that comes in order, like words in a sentence or readings over time.
A network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward.
An RNN with gates that decide what to remember and forget, so it keeps information longer.
A simpler gated RNN, like a lighter LSTM.
A model that reads one sequence and writes another, like translating a sentence.
During training, giving the model the true previous word rather than its own guess.
Getting computers to work with human language.
A piece of text a language model reads or writes: a word, part of a word or a mark.
The tool that cuts text into tokens and turns them into numbers.
A way to build a tokenizer by repeatedly joining the most common pairs of pieces.
The full list of tokens a model knows; GPT-2 has 50,257.
An early way to learn word embeddings from which words appear near each other.
A very large model trained on text to predict the next token; chat assistants are built on them.
A family of language models that write text one token at a time; GPT-2 is a 2019 one.
A language model that reads text in both directions, used for understanding rather than writing.
The first, long training on huge amounts of general data.
Further training of a pre-trained model on a smaller, specific dataset.
Reusing what a model learned on one task to help with another.
Fine-tuning by learning a small add-on to each weight matrix instead of changing it all.
Fine-tuning a language model on examples of following instructions.
Training a language model with rewards learned from people's preferences between answers.
Learning from preferred and rejected answers directly, without a separate reward model.
The text given to a language model for it to continue or answer.
How many tokens a model can look at at once; GPT-2's is 1,024.
How surprised a language model is by real text, on average; lower is better.
Choosing the next token at random according to the model's chances.
A dial on sampling: low makes the model pick its top choice, high makes it more random.
Sampling only from the k likeliest tokens, or from the likeliest ones that add up to p.
Always picking the single likeliest next token.
Keeping several of the best partial answers at once and extending them all.
When a language model confidently says something false or made up.
Letting each token look at the others and take in what is relevant to it.
Attention where a sequence looks at itself.
Attention where one sequence looks at another, like a translation looking back at the source.
In attention, what each token asks for, what it offers to be found by, and what it passes on.
Several attentions side by side, each free to look for different things.
The network design behind modern language models: attention plus small MLPs, stacked in blocks.
Stopping each token from looking at later tokens, so a model cannot peek at the answer.
Numbers added so a transformer knows the order of the tokens.
Telling attention where tokens sit by rotating their queries and keys.
Telling attention about distance by lowering scores for far-away tokens.
A layer of many small networks where each token only uses a few, saving work.
A sequence model that carries a running summary forward, as an alternative to attention.
A state space model that chooses what to keep as it reads.
The running list of numbers each layer of a transformer reads from and adds to.
An attention head that spots repeated patterns and copies what came next last time.
Opening a model up to understand how it reaches its answers.
An autoencoder used to split a model's inner numbers into fewer, clearer features.
A computer somewhere else that answers requests sent to it over the internet.
The program on your device that sends requests to a server and shows the replies.
A message sent to a server, and the answer it sends back.
A fixed way for one program to ask another for something, like asking a model a question.
A simple text format for structured data, used to send requests and replies.
The rules web browsers and servers use to send requests and replies.
Sending each piece of the reply as soon as it is ready instead of waiting for the end.
Keeping each token's keys and values so a model need not re-read the whole text for every new token.
The two phases of answering: reading the whole prompt at once, then writing one token at a time.
Running many people's requests through the model together, so its weights are read once for all.
How much work gets done per second, and how long one answer takes to arrive.
A program that uses a model in a loop, letting it call tools, read the results and keep going.
Text from a model asking the program around it to do something, like read a file or run tests.
Tokens a model writes for itself before its answer, often hidden, but counted.
A setting for how much a model may think before answering: more effort, more tokens, more time.
Letting a small model guess several tokens and a big one check them all at once, to answer faster.
A way to compute attention in tiles so it needs far less memory.
A computer's main chip: a few fast cores that are good at anything.
A chip with thousands of small cores, very fast at the matrix maths of neural networks.
The fast memory on a GPU, where the model's weights must sit while it runs.
One addition or multiplication of decimal numbers; used to count a model's work.
One multiply and one add, the basic step of a matrix product.
A picture of whether a computation is slowed by arithmetic or by moving data.
Training on several devices at once, each with a copy of the model and its own share of the data.
Splitting one model across several devices, by cutting its layers or its matrices.
Splitting the optimizer's memory across devices so no copy is repeated.
Saving memory in training by forgetting some inner numbers and working them out again later.
Ways of storing a decimal number in 4 or 2 bytes; fewer bytes are faster but less precise.
Storing each number as a whole number in one byte, to make a model smaller and faster.
Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits so it takes less memory.
Training a model while pretending its numbers are stored with fewer bits, so it copes when they are.
Training with 16-bit numbers where it is safe and 32-bit where it matters.
Removing the weights or parts of a model that matter least, to make it smaller.
Training a small model to copy a big model's answers.
How a model's loss improves, predictably, as its size, data and compute grow.
Learning by trying actions and getting rewards, rather than from right answers.
In reinforcement learning, the learner that acts in a world and collects rewards.
The score an RL agent gets for what it did; it learns to get more of it.
An RL agent's rule for choosing an action in each situation.
Learning how good each action is in each situation, from rewards.
Q-learning with a neural network, as used to play video games.
A steady way to improve a policy, used in RLHF.
Planning by trying out many possible futures and favouring the promising ones.
The simplest RL problem: choose between options whose payouts you must discover.
An agent scoring well by exploiting a flaw in the reward instead of doing the task.
HEP's name for using a trained classifier (BDT or DNN) on many variables at once.
The ROOT library long used in HEP to train BDTs and neural networks.
A classifier's output score, used as one variable to separate signal from background.
Selecting events with a list of hand-chosen thresholds on variables instead of a trained classifier.
A chosen threshold on a classifier, fixed by a target efficiency, like the 70% working point.
The events you are looking for, and everything else that looks like them.
The share of real signal events a selection keeps.
The share of background a selection throws away, often given as 1 over the share kept.
aka: Specificity, true negative rate; or 1 / false positive rate

plain: How often background is wrongly tagged as signal, as in b-tagging.
Comparing a classifier's scores on training and test samples to spot overfitting.
One recorded collision (or simulated one): the unit HEP classifies.
aka: Example, instance: one row of data

plain: A number saying how much a simulated event counts, to match real data; not a network weight.
Simulated events made with random numbers to model what the detector should see.
Many fake datasets drawn at random from a model, to see how results scatter.
A single made-up dataset where every bin holds exactly its expected count, used for quick sensitivity estimates.
Where you look for the signal, and nearby regions with little signal used to measure the background.
A region next to the signal region, used to estimate the background underneath it.
Searching a mass spectrum for a small peak on a smooth background.
How many standard deviations a result is from background-only; roughly s / √b for a simple count.
HEP's bar for claiming a discovery: a 1 in 3.5 million chance that background alone fakes it.
Looking in many places makes a chance bump more likely somewhere, so the significance must be corrected.
HEP's method for upper limits that avoids excluding signals the search could not see.
The largest signal still compatible with the data, at a chosen confidence.
An upper-limit plot with green and yellow bands for the expected limit's spread.
A quantity you must allow for but do not care about, like an energy scale uncertainty.
An uncertainty from how the measurement was made, not from random counting.
Handling nuisance parameters by re-fitting them for each value of the quantity you care about.
Fitting a model to each event's value, or to counts in histogram bins.
When a selection or classifier bends the shape of a distribution, such as faking a peak.
Looking for anything unexpected rather than one predicted signal, often with autoencoders.
A spray of particles from one quark or gluon, recorded together in the detector.
Identifying jets from bottom quarks, a classic HEP classification task done with ML.
Extra collisions recorded at the same time as the one of interest.
The fast first selection that decides which collisions to keep; increasingly runs ML on FPGAs.
A network that works on points and their links, used in HEP for tracks, jets and particle clouds.
CERN's data-analysis software, the long-time standard file format and toolkit in HEP.
A file format for trained networks, used to run Python-trained models inside C++ HEP software.
Choosing a model's parameters so it matches the data; machine learning calls this training.
A program that finds the parameters giving the smallest loss.
CERN's minimiser, used for HEP fits since the 1970s.
Minuit for Python: you give it a function and a start, and it finds the minimum and the errors.
Minuit's main minimiser: it feels the slope by probing each parameter, steps, and builds up the curvature as it goes.
Minuit's step that measures the curvature at the minimum, giving the error bars and their correlations.
Minuit's step for uneven error bars: walk each parameter out, re-fitting the rest, until the loss rises enough.
A minimiser that uses no slopes at all: a small shape of points that rolls and shrinks downhill.
Minuit's estimate of how far the loss still is above its minimum; it stops when this is tiny.
How much the loss must rise to mark one standard deviation: 1 for chi-square, 0.5 for −log L.
The table of second derivatives: how curved the loss is along and between every pair of parameters.
How uncertain each fitted parameter is and how their errors move together; it comes from the inverse of the Hessian.
How much two quantities move together, from −1 to 1.
Stepping straight to where a bowl with the measured slope and curvature would have its bottom.
A Newton-like method that learns the curvature from its own steps instead of computing it, like MIGRAD or BFGS.
Trying a few step lengths along one direction to find a good one.
Estimating a slope by evaluating the loss a little either side of a point, as Minuit does.
Getting exact slopes by applying the chain rule to every step of the code, as neural-network libraries do.
A minimiser that uses curvature as well as slope, so it takes fewer, better-aimed steps.
The point where further steps no longer improve the fit, by the minimiser's own test.
A dip that is lowest only nearby, against the lowest point of all.
A flat point that is a minimum in some directions and a maximum in others.
Bowl-shaped everywhere, so there is only one minimum; a straight-line fit's chi-square is convex.
The loss drawn over the parameters, with its valleys, ridges and minima.
How differently curved the loss is in different directions; badly conditioned losses are slow to minimise.
Using all the data for every step (classic fits, Minuit) or a few examples (SGD).
The noisy path of SGD: each step is a little off, but the errors average out around the minimum.
Where a minimiser begins; a poor start can land it in the wrong minimum.
Using data to estimate parameters and how sure we are of them; ML's 'inference' means prediction instead.
How probable the observed data are for given parameter values.
Minus the log of the likelihood; minimising it is maximum likelihood.
A recipe that turns data into a value for a parameter; a fit and a trained model's prediction are both one.
How far an estimator's average lands from the truth; not a network's bias.
How much an estimator would scatter if the data were collected again.
How far a measured or fitted value might be from the truth, usually one standard deviation.
A range built so that, in repeated experiments, it would hold the truth a stated share of the time.
How often an interval method really holds the truth, against how often it claims to.
What you believe before seeing the data, and after; Bayes' theorem links them.
The Bayesian range that holds the parameter with a stated probability, given the data and prior.
The most probable parameters given the data and a prior; an L2-regularised fit is one with a Gaussian prior.
Two schools: probability as long-run frequency, or as degree of belief.
The difference between a data point and the model at that point.
A difference divided by its uncertainty; pulls of a good fit spread with width 1.
Whether a fit describes the data well, such as chi-square per degree of freedom near 1.
The number of data points minus the number of fitted parameters.
How counts of rare, independent events scatter; HEP's counting statistics.
The bell curve; sums of many small effects end up shaped like it.
Working out the uncertainty of a result from the uncertainties of its inputs.
Estimating an uncertainty by refitting many datasets resampled from your own data.
Deciding between two explanations of the data, such as background only or signal plus background.
One number computed from the data that a hypothesis test is based on.
Rejecting a true hypothesis (a false alarm) and keeping a false one (a miss).
How much more probable the data are under one hypothesis than another.
The likelihood ratio is the best possible test between two hypotheses; a well-trained classifier learns it.
Several models whose answers are combined, often better than any one.
The quantity a fit is really after, like a signal strength, as opposed to nuisance parameters.
How much signal there is compared with the prediction: 1 means as predicted, 0 means none.
Fitting data as a sum of predicted shapes, one per process, scaling each.
A likelihood that also fits the total number of events, not only their shape.
How likely a process is in each collision, measured in barns.
How many collisions a dataset holds; times a cross-section it gives the expected number of events.
The overall size of a predicted distribution, such as cross-section times luminosity; not a normalisation layer.
Correcting a detector's measured values so they match the true ones; not ML calibration.
A correction that makes simulation match data, such as for a tagging efficiency.
How well simulation matches real data; models trained on simulation depend on it.
Making a model trained on one kind of data, like simulation, work on another, like real data.
Removing detector effects from a measured distribution to estimate the true one.
A combination of particles' energies and momenta that peaks at the mass of the particle they came from.
Variables built by physicists, like an invariant mass, against raw ones, like each particle's momentum.
Training a classifier so its output does not depend on a variable like mass, so it cannot sculpt it.
What really happened in a simulated event, known because we simulated it; the labels ML trains on.
A table, built from simulation, of how often events from each true bin are measured in each bin.
How many unweighted events a weighted sample is worth: (Σw)² ÷ Σw².
Measuring an efficiency in data: one object (the tag) picks clean events; the other (the probe) is tested.
The significance a typical experiment would get: the median over toys, or one Asimov dataset.
Training a classifier to tell simulation from data, then weighting each simulated event by s / (1 − s).
A network that runs on each item of a set, adds the results up, then reads the sum: order cannot matter.
An answer that stays the same however the inputs are ordered, as a set's should.
Training many times on resampled data and taking the spread of the answers as an error bar.
